title: Spring AOP Proxies Revision Handbook
summary: Quick revision notes on Spring AOP: aspects, advice types, pointcuts, JDK vs CGLIB proxies, the self-invocation trap, and how proxies power @Transactional, security and caching.

chapters.title: AOP Concepts and the Proxy Mental Model
points: Aspect = a class (@Aspect + @Component) bundling cross-cutting logic such as logging, transactions or security away from business code
Join point = a point in execution; in Spring AOP it is always a method execution on a Spring bean (no field or constructor join points)
Pointcut = predicate selecting join points; advice = the code run at them; an advisor pairs one pointcut with one advice
Mental model: Spring wraps the target bean in a proxy; callers get the proxy, the proxy runs advice, then delegates to the real target
Weaving happens at runtime via proxies created by a BeanPostProcessor at startup; AspectJ instead weaves bytecode at compile or load time and supports field, constructor and self-call join points

chapters.title: Advice Types and Pointcut Expressions
points: Five advice types: @Before, @AfterReturning (returning=), @AfterThrowing (throwing=), @After (finally-style, always runs), @Around
@Around takes ProceedingJoinPoint and must call proceed() and return its result; it can skip, retry, modify args or swallow exceptions; it is the only type that controls execution
Order on success: Around-before, Before, method, AfterReturning, After, Around-after; on exception AfterThrowing replaces AfterReturning
Pointcut designators: execution(* com.app.service.*.*(..)), within(com.app.service..*), @annotation(com.app.Audited), @within, args(), bean(orderService)
Example: @Around("@annotation(Timed)") public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { long t=System.nanoTime(); try { return pjp.proceed(); } finally { log(System.nanoTime()-t); } }

Mistake: @Around that forgets to return proceed() makes the caller get null; use the weakest advice type that does the job; multiple aspects are ordered with @Order (lower value runs first on the way in)

chapters.title: JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB
points: JDK dynamic proxy: java.lang.reflect.Proxy implements the target's interfaces and dispatches through an InvocationHandler; requires at least one interface and the proxy is not an instance of the concrete class
CGLIB proxy: generates a runtime subclass of the target class and overrides methods; works with no interface and the proxy is an instance of the target class
Spring Boot 2+ defaults to CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true); plain Spring uses JDK proxy when the bean has interfaces, else CGLIB; force with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass=true)
CGLIB limits: final classes cannot be proxied and final or private methods are not intercepted (the call runs on the proxy instance whose fields are unset, so state may be null)

Mistake: injecting by concrete class under a JDK proxy gives 'BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException'; inject the interface or use CGLIB; call getClass() on a bean to check, it shows $$SpringCGLIB or jdk.proxy

chapters.title: Self-Invocation: Why @Transactional and @Cacheable Get Skipped
points: Advice lives in the proxy, not in the target; a call from this.method() inside the same bean goes straight to the target and bypasses the proxy entirely
Example: public void outer(){ this.inner(); } with @Transactional on inner(): outer is called through the proxy but inner runs with no new transaction, no REQUIRES_NEW, no rollback rules
Same cause explains skipped @Cacheable, @Async, @Retryable and @PreAuthorize on internal calls
Fix 1 (preferred): move inner() to another bean and inject it, so the call crosses a proxy boundary
Fix 2: inject self via @Lazy or ApplicationContext, or call AopContext.currentProxy() with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy=true); Fix 3: AspectJ weaving mode (mode=ASPECTJ) which has no proxy

Related gotchas: @Transactional on private or package-private methods is ignored under proxies (public needed for default proxy rules), and a class not created by Spring (new Foo()) has no proxy at all

chapters.title: How Proxies Power Transactions, Security and Caching
points: @Transactional: TransactionInterceptor (an @Around advice) gets a connection, begins, calls proceed(), commits on return, rolls back on RuntimeException/Error only; checked exceptions need rollbackFor

Transaction state is bound to the thread (TransactionSynchronizationManager), so @Transactional does not propagate into new threads or @Async tasks; propagation REQUIRED joins an existing transaction, REQUIRES_NEW suspends it
Security: @PreAuthorize/@Secured need @EnableMethodSecurity; a MethodInterceptor checks the SecurityContext before proceed() and throws AccessDeniedException; @PostAuthorize checks the returned value
Caching: CacheInterceptor checks the cache by key before proceed(); @Cacheable stores the result on a miss, @CachePut always runs and updates, @CacheEvict removes entries; needs @EnableCaching

Mistake: swallowing an exception inside a @Transactional method (catch without rethrow) means the proxy sees normal return and commits; also the interceptor order matters, e.g. caching a result before the transaction commits

chapters.title: Spring AOP Cheat Sheet
points: Advice cheat table: Before, AfterReturning, AfterThrowing, After, Around, with when each runs and whether it can change the result
Pointcut quick forms: execution(* pkg..*.*(..)), within(pkg..*), @annotation(X), args(String), bean(name)
Proxy choice: interface present and not forced means JDK, otherwise CGLIB; Boot defaults to CGLIB; no final classes or methods
Proxy-bypass checklist: self-invocation, private or final methods, new-created objects, non-Spring-managed beans, annotation missing its @Enable switch
Annotation switches: @EnableTransactionManagement, @EnableCaching, @EnableMethodSecurity, @EnableAsync, @EnableAspectJAutoProxy
